Score candidate cell counts on several criteria

Source: R/resolution-profile.R
resolution_profile.Rd

Scores candidate numbers of cells (levels) for a layer of points, so that the count chosen, by select_resolution() or by eye, can be defended with the whole profile in place of one criterion's optimum.

Usage

resolution_profile(
  data_sf,
  response_var = NULL,
  predictor_vars = NULL,
  levels = NULL,
  n_levels = 20L,
  min_cell_n = 9L,
  sample_n = 1500L,
  nstart = NULL,
  seed = 123L,
  sac = "auto",
  select_on = c("all", "split"),
  range_floor = FALSE,
  partition = c("density", "kmeans"),
  init = c("kmeans++", "random"),
  density_power = 1,
  density_k = 8L,
  iter_max = NULL,
  estimate = "auto",
  obs_per_cell = "auto"
)

# S3 method for class 'resolution_profile'
print(x, digits = 3L, ...)

Arguments

data_sf

An sf object of points (other geometries are reduced to representative points with coerce_to_points()). Features without a location, as given, once projected or in the CRS of sac, are dropped with a warning, and a layer that mixes XY and XYZ geometries or carries M is read in x and y (see spatialkit-geometry).

response_var

Name of the response column (numeric or logical), or NULL. Enables cp and moran_z, and, when it is numeric, the pooled estimate the default profile scores by loo. A variogram estimated from it also gives the range floor the bounds report and reliability; it is estimated on a ladder of counts or when sac asks for it, and not on the default ladder of one size, so cp and reliability are NA there. Rows where it, or a predictor, is missing or non-finite stay in the geometry and are left out of the OLS fit, the RSS, cp, moran_z and the count the support ceiling divides by min_cell_n; a logged warning gives their number, and an R warning says so when they lower the ceiling.

predictor_vars

Optional predictor column names (numeric or logical). With them, cp scores the OLS residuals of the response on the predictors, the variogram is estimated from those residuals, and moran_z regresses the cell means on the cell-mean predictors.

levels

Optional integer vector of level counts to score, replacing the ladder; values below 2, above the number of distinct locations, or at or above the number of points, are dropped (k-means cannot place more centres than there are distinct points, and stats::kmeans() refuses as many centres as points). When none is left the call stops with an error, before the variogram is estimated or read, so it raises no warning about the variogram.

n_levels

Number of levels on the ladder. Default 20. The ladder has fewer when rounding puts two of them on one count, and one more when the range floor is added as a level (see "The ladder and its bounds"). Supplying it, or min_cell_n, sample_n, levels or range_floor, gives that ladder in place of the ladder of sizes obs_per_cell = "auto" would set.

min_cell_n

Minimum average number of rows per cell that a level must keep (scored rows when response_var is given: those with a response and every predictor; points otherwise); sets the ceiling. Default 9. A layer that cannot give two cells that many is profiled at two cells, or at the levels asked for, with supported = FALSE and a warning. It is floored to a whole number, and it is not read on a ladder obs_per_cell sets (see "The ladder and its bounds").

sample_n

Points are subsampled to this many before the k-means fits, as in determine_optimal_levels(), on the ladder of "The ladder and its bounds"; on a ladder of sizes, the default, the centres are fitted to every row. Default 1500. The columns read off the fitted cells (wss, the cell_ and cells_ columns, rss, moran_i, moran_z) describe the subsample; the bounds, supported, the variance term of cp and reliability describe the whole layer, so the answer does not change with sample_n except through the fits. The fits are those of the subsample, which seed draws, so on a layer of more than sample_n points the count read off the profile can move with seed and with sample_n. The level select_resolution() chooses off such a profile without an estimate is refitted to every point before its seeds are handed on (see refit_rows under "Value"); a profile with an estimate scores it on every row in the cells of the centres fitted, and hands those centres on.

nstart

Starts per level; the best is kept. They are k-means++ starts unless init says otherwise. NULL (default) is the kind's own number: 3 for the kind "density" and 25 for the kind "kmeans". A number is run under either partition. attr(, "nstart") holds the number that was run.

seed

RNG seed for the subsample and the restarts; restored afterwards. Default 123. The rows are put in coordinate order before either, so the profile does not depend on the order they come in. Each level's restarts run on a stream of their own, seeded from seed and the level, so for one seed a level gets the same cells on any ladder that holds it and is fitted to the same rows, and with them the same wss, rss, moran_z and the other columns read off its cells. On a layer of more than sample_n rows a ladder of counts is fitted to a subsample and a ladder of sizes to every row, so there the two can give a level other cells. cp also reads its noise variance, which without a usable variogram comes from the ladder's finest level (attr(, "cp_noise")).

sac

Optional sac_range object from estimate_sac_range() to take the range, nugget and correlation function from. Pass one fitted with detrend = "reml", say. It must describe the variable the profile scores: the raw response without predictor_vars, the residuals on them with; a sac whose detrended attribute says otherwise is used with a warning. Its range is read in its own CRS (attr(sac, "crs")), to which the points are transformed first, so the area, the floor and cell_diam_median are then in that CRS's units. A sac whose range was rejected (NA with a rejected_reason) gives cp its nugget (held to the semivariance of nearest-neighbour pairs, and not at all when it is at the fit's lower bound), with a warning, and leaves reliability NA, since that needs the range; one whose model did not converge (its fit has no minimum inside the ranges searched, so its nugget and sill are not fitted values), or whose range is below the shortest lag fitted (a structure that cannot be told from a nugget, so the nugget is not identified either), gives neither, and cp takes its noise variance from the finest level (see cp above). Whether the model converged is read from the model (attr(attr(sac, "variogram_model"), "converged"), which estimate_sac_range() sets and describes), not from the reason: the reason names one ground for the refusal, and such a fit is refused as past the largest lag. The warning then names both. A sac that carries no such flag (one made by hand, or built from REML parameters) is judged by its reason. Under select_on = "split" the sac must come from the selection half alone: run the profile once without it, fit the sac on data_sf[attr(p, "split")$selection, ] and pass it to a second call with the same seed, which makes the same split. When NULL and a response is given, one is estimated on the subsample (its selection half under "split") with the same predictor_vars. A plain number is taken as the range alone, in the units of the CRS the profile is computed in (metres for lon/lat input): it gives the range floor, reliability, which needs a fitted model, is NA, and cp takes its noise variance from the finest level whose cells hold at least two scored rows on average (see cp above). A sac refused because the response shows no spatial structure (either of the two rejected_reason values of estimate_sac_range() that say so; the model it attaches is a pure nugget) gives cp no nugget either, and select_resolution() then returns structured = FALSE. A units object is refused rather than read as a number in whatever unit it was written in. The string "auto", the default, is NULL on every ladder but one that obs_per_cell sets. On that ladder no variogram is estimated or read: cp and reliability are NA at every level, cp takes no noise variance from the finest level in its place, attr(, "cp_noise") is a list whose source is "none" and whose reason says why, and the variogram and sac attributes are NULL. The other columns do not read the variogram and are the numbers sac = NULL gives. sac = NULL estimates the variogram on a ladder of sizes too, and gives cp and reliability there.

select_on

"all" (default) profiles every point; "split" reads the response on one spatially blocked half only (the OLS fit, the variogram, rss, cp and moran_z) and returns the other half as the set to estimate on, in the "split" attribute. The cells, wss, elbow, and the extent and point counts behind the bounds, cp's variance term and reliability still come from every point, because the tessellation the count is for is built on every point: the levels are cell counts for the whole layer, and the estimation half's response never touches them. See the "Post-selection inference" section of determine_optimal_levels; the profile reads the response whenever response_var is given.

range_floor

FALSE (default) starts the ladder at 2 whatever the range, and the range floor is reported in the bounds and the print without being applied. TRUE starts the ladder at the floor when the data support it and the floor is below the ceiling; an estimated range then sets the fewest cells any criterion can choose (see "The ladder and its bounds").

partition

What the centres of the cells minimise, at every level of the ladder. "density" (default): the sum of squared distances from the points to their nearest centre, each point weighted by its local density to the power density_power; compact cells that, at the default power, hold about the same number of points each once there are more cells than dense places, and counts about as uneven as "kmeans" gives below that. "kmeans": the same sum unweighted; compact cells whose counts are several times higher in dense places than in sparse ones, from 25 starts under nstart = NULL. See "The partition".

init

How each start is drawn. "kmeans++" (default): the centres one at a time, each in proportion to its squared distance from those already drawn, times its weight under partition = "density". "random": k distinct locations at random, as kmeans() draws them.

density_power

For partition = "density": the power the local density is raised to for a point's weight, a number from 0 to 2. Default 1, which evens out the cell counts once the cells outnumber the dense places (see "The partition"). 0 weights every point alike, the objective of "kmeans" (reached by Lloyd's iteration, so the centres are close to that kind's and not equal to them); values between give counts between the two; values above 1 give the cells of dense places fewer points than those of sparse places. Setting it under partition = "kmeans", which does not read it, is a warning.

density_k

For partition = "density": the number of nearest neighbours the local density is read from. Default 8. It is held to one fewer than the distinct locations. A small number follows the density closely and noisily; a large one smooths it. Setting it under partition = "kmeans" is a warning.

iter_max

The most iterations a start runs for: a single positive whole number, or NULL (default) for the kind's own limit, 50 for partition = "kmeans" from k-means++ starts and 100 for random starts and for partition = "density". A kept start that was cut off at the limit is a warning of class "spatialkit_not_converged", except for the kind "kmeans" from k-means++ starts under iter_max = NULL, which reports nothing.

estimate

The cell value the profile scores, which is the one summarize_by_cell() is to report: "auto" (default; see below), NULL for none, "mean" for the plain mean of a cell's rows, "pooled" for the mean pulled toward the mean of the 8 nearest cells. With an estimate the profile gains five columns and attr(, "estimate") (see "Value"), and every column and attribute it has without one is unchanged. loo is the leave-one-out mean squared error of that estimate: each row predicted by the value of its cell computed without it. Under "mean" a row in a cell of two or more is predicted by the mean of the others, and a row alone in its cell by the mean of the cell of its nearest other row. Under "pooled" the cell's mean and its own weight are computed again without the row, and the spread inside the cells, the spread between a cell and its target, and the targets are held. It is computed on every row of the layer with a finite response (of the selection half under select_on = "split"), not on the subsample the centres were fitted to, and each row is scored in the cell of its nearest centre, the cell get_voronoi_seeds() hands on. It needs no variogram. Rows at one location are left out one at a time. "auto" is "pooled" when there is a numeric response_var with a finite value and no predictor_vars, and NULL otherwise. NULL scores none and gives the profile without the five columns. "mean" and "pooled" are errors without a response_var, with predictor_vars (the profile would then score residuals, and the summary reports cell values of the response), with a logical response, and with a response that has no finite value. Under select_on = "split" a selection half with no finite response is not an error: the five columns are NA at every level, with a warning of class spatialkit_no_scored_rows.

obs_per_cell

Rows per cell: "auto" (default; see below); NULL for the ladder described under "The ladder and its bounds", whatever the other arguments are; or one number or several, each at least 1 (fractions are allowed), for a ladder of sizes. The level of a size \(s\) is max(2, round(n / s)) cells, with \(n\) the rows that have a response (and, with predictor_vars, every predictor), or every point when there is no response_var or no row has a response. Under select_on = "split" \(n\) counts the rows of both halves, since the cells are built on every point. On a ladder of sizes the centres are fitted to every row, no subsample is drawn, and n_levels, min_cell_n, sample_n and range_floor are not read: supplying n_levels, min_cell_n, sample_n or range_floor = TRUE beside a numeric obs_per_cell is a warning of class spatialkit_ladder_unused, and levels beside it is an error. A level is held to the most centres k-means can place (the distinct locations, and one short of the points). "auto" is NULL when levels is given or the caller supplies any of those four arguments; otherwise 4.5 when the estimate is "pooled", the seven sizes 18, 12, 9, 6, 4.5, 3 and 2 when it is "mean", and NULL without an estimate. The cost of a ladder of sizes is bounded before any fit (see "Conditions").

x

A resolution_profile, for print().

digits

For print(): significant digits for the table. Default 3.

...

Ignored.

Value

A data.frame of class resolution_profile, one row per level. Columns a missing input leaves undefined are NA.

levels

The number of cells.

wss

The within-cell sum of squares of the coordinates, every point counted once, under either partition.

wss_spread

The relative spread of WSS across the restarts; under partition = "density", of the weighted sum the starts minimise.

elbow

The sag of the WSS curve below a power law (see "The criteria").

cell_n_min, cell_n_median

The fewest and the median points per cell.

cell_diam_median

Twice the median RMS radius of the cells, in coordinate units: about 0.8 of the side of a square cell of the same area, and less for finer cells, so a size to compare levels by rather than a width.

rss, cp

The residual sum of squares of the scored rows about their cell means, and Mallows' \(C_p\).

moran_i, moran_z

Moran's I of the cell means and its standardised deviate.

reliability

The between-cell signal's share of the spread in the cell means.

cells_resp

The cells that hold at least one scored row.

cell_resp_mean

The scored rows per such cell; compare it with min_cell_n.

Like the other columns read off the fitted cells, cells_resp and cell_resp_mean count rows of the subsample when the layer is larger than sample_n: the cells of the layer then hold about n_response / n_scored times as many scored rows as cell_resp_mean shows (under select_on = "split", split$n_response / n_scored: both count the rows of the selection half).

With an estimate the frame has five more columns, after cell_resp_mean:

scored_per_cell

The rows loo read over the cells that hold one; the layer's counterpart of cell_resp_mean, which counts the subsample's rows.

loo

The leave-one-out mean squared error of the estimate; lower is better.

loo_se

The standard error over rows of that level's mean squared error. It is not the standard error of a difference between two levels, whose errors come from the same rows.

share_alone

The share of the scored rows that are the only scored row of their cell.

own_weight

The median over cells of the weight a pooled value gives the cell's own mean; NA under "mean".

loo, loo_se and own_weight are NA at a level where no cell holds two scored rows, at every level when the response is constant over the rows loo reads, and at every level when those rows' values lie beyond what the arithmetic of the estimate holds (spatialkit_pool_unavailable). All five are NA at every level when no row of the selection half has a response (select_on = "split"; spatialkit_no_scored_rows).

Attributes:

bounds

A list: floor, ceiling, ceiling_from ("min_cell_n", "min_cell_n (rows with a response)", "distinct locations", "sample_n", "fewer than two supported cells" or "fewer than two distinct locations", whichever bound it), supported, area, range, n (the points in the layer), n_sample (the points the k-means fits ran on), n_distinct, min_cell_n, range_floor, n_response (the rows of the layer that carry a response and, with predictor_vars, every predictor, which the support ceiling counts; NA without a response_var), n_scored (the rows of the subsample the response criteria read; NA without a response_var), levels_given (whether levels set the ladder), predictors (whether predictor_vars were given) and, where rows have a response and none of them every predictor, n_response_only (the rows with a finite response). On a ladder that obs_per_cell sets, bounds describes that ladder: ceiling is the finest level; ceiling_from is "obs_per_cell", "distinct locations", "fewer than two cells of the size" or "fewer than two distinct locations"; supported is FALSE when the finest size gives fewer than two cells or the range floor is above the finest level; levels_given is TRUE; n_sample is every point; min_cell_n holds the argument, which is not read; and two fields are added, obs_per_cell (the sizes, largest first) and size_levels (the level of each, named by size; NA for a size of "auto" that gives fewer than two cells and was left out).

variogram

A list with nugget, psill, range (NA when rejected), model and detrended (whether the sac says it is a variogram of residuals; NA when it does not say); NULL when none was usable.

variable

"response", "residuals" or NA.

wss_bumps, nstart

The number of rising steps on the WSS curve, and the starts run per level.

sac

The range object used.

split

With select_on = "split": a spatialkit_split with selection and estimation (integer row positions in data_sf), the method and seed that made them, and with a response n_response, the rows of the selection half with a finite response and every predictor, counted on the layer before any subsample.

cp_noise

A list with source ("variogram nugget", "finest-level residual mean square" or "short-lag semivariance"), value (the \(\tau^2\) used) and level (the level it was read at, or NA). Under the short-lag semivariance it also has cap, that semivariance, and uncapped, a list of the source, value and level it held. When the finest level whose cells hold two scored rows on average has a residual mean square of 0 to within rounding, source and value are NA, and the list has level (that level), rows_per_cell (its scored rows a cell), rms (its residual mean square: 0, or the rounding it was read as) and reason, which select_resolution() gives. On a ladder of sizes under sac = "auto" it is a list whose source is "none" and whose reason says why. NULL when cp has no noise variance for another reason; see cp under "The criteria".

one_cell

What one cell for the whole layer scores, the reference a level has to beat: a list with n (the scored rows), rss (their total sum of squares), cp (the same formula at one cell, or NA when cp has no noise variance), constant (whether the scored variable is constant to within rounding), cp_levels (the cp column it belongs to) and f_p (named by level, the p-value of the F test of that level's cell means against one mean, \((TSS - RSS) / (L - 1)\) over \(RSS / (m - L)\) on the \(L\) cells that hold a scored row and the \(m\) scored rows). NULL without a response.

centres, centres_crs, hull

A list named by level of the two-column matrices of the scored partitions' centres, the CRS they are in, and the convex hull of the points profiled (an sfc in that CRS). A k-means partition is the Voronoi partition of its centres, so these seed the cells each level was scored on: select_resolution() returns the chosen level's as $seeds, and get_voronoi_seeds() and voronoi_seeds_kmeans() use them when given the selection or the profile. The centres carry the hull as their "cover" attribute, which those two functions hand on so that Voronoi cells built on the seeds reach the edge of the points.

refit_rows

When the centres were fitted to a subsample and the profile has no estimate: a list with xy, the coordinates of every point in the CRS of the centres, and iter_max, the iteration limit of the fits, from which select_resolution() refits the level it chooses to every point. The seeds are then the chosen level's centres refitted to every point, whose cells are not the cells scored (see select_resolution, "Value").

partition

On a profile built with partition = "density" or init = "random": a list with kind, init, density_power and density_k (both NA for kind = "kmeans"); for kind = "density", objective, the weighted sum the centres minimise, named by level; iter_max, the iteration limit; and iter and converged, the iterations each level's kept start took and whether it stopped before the limit, named by level. The selection carries the first four as $partition, its seeds and the seeds the seeding functions return as attr(, "partition"), and a Voronoi tessellation built on them as params$partition. A profile of the kind "kmeans" from k-means++ starts has no such attribute, and neither has anything made from it.

estimate

With an estimate: a list with value ("mean" or "pooled"), neighbours (8, or NA under "mean"), response (the column), n (the rows loo read), rows ("all" or "selection half"), features ("points", or "other" when the layer held features that were reduced to points), seed, constant, loo_one_cell and loo_one_cell_se (the same error with one mean for all those rows, the reference a level has to beat; NA for a constant response, for fewer than two rows and for values beyond the arithmetic of the estimate), loo_levels (the loo column those references belong to, named by level), and, named by level, sigma2 (the spread of the rows about their cell's mean), tau2 (the mean squared distance between a cell's level and its target; NA under "mean"), cells (the cells that hold a scored row) and f_p (the p-value of the F test of those cells' means against one mean). constant says whether the response is constant over those rows by the estimate's test, which reads the raw values and the values centred on their median and scaled, so that 1e15 plus a spread of 1 is not constant while values that differ only by their rounding, 0.1 beside 0.3 / 3, are; it is FALSE for fewer than two rows. one_cell$constant, the test for cp, reads the scored rows of the subsample the same way, and residuals against the rounding of the regression and of the response.

Details

Called with a numeric response, no predictors and none of levels, n_levels, min_cell_n, sample_n or range_floor, the profile is one level: the count that gives 4.5 rows per cell (obs_per_cell = "auto"), scored for pooled values (estimate = "auto") by the leave-one-out error loo, with no variogram fitted (sac = "auto"), in cells of the density kind (partition = "density") kept from 3 k-means++ starts (nstart = NULL). cp and reliability need the variogram and elbow needs a curve, so the three are NA there; moran_z is computed. select_resolution() reads the count off it by the size.

Any of those five ladder arguments, obs_per_cell = NULL, or a call with no estimate (no response, predictor_vars, or a logical or wholly missing response) gives a ladder of counts (see "The ladder and its bounds"). At every level the profile then scores the within-cluster sum of squares of the coordinates and its elbow, Mallows' \(C_p\) of the piecewise-constant approximation of the response by cell means, Moran's \(z\) of the cell means and their reliability, and, with an estimate, the leave-one-out error of the cell value. Mallows (1973) presents \(C_p\) itself as a display of the bias-variance trade-off across candidates, and the profile is that display, with the other criteria alongside.

print() gives a header that states the ladder and its bounds, the variogram (or why none was fitted), what was scored and on how many starts, what one cell for the whole layer scores, the estimate, whether the WSS curve has an elbow and, under select_on = "split", the rows of each half; then the table, one row per level, at digits significant digits.

The partition

The cells at every level are the Voronoi cells of a set of centres: a point belongs to the centre nearest to it. partition says what the centres minimise, and every level of the ladder is built with the same kind.

"kmeans"

The sum, over the points, of the squared distance to the nearest centre. The centres follow the square root of the point density. The cells are compact, smaller where the points are dense and larger where they are sparse, and a cell in a dense place holds several times the points of a cell in a sparse place.

"density" (default)

The same sum with each point weighted by its local density to the power density_power. The local density at a point is the number of points in the disc that reaches its density_k-th nearest neighbour, over the area of that disc. With density_power = 1 the centres follow the point density itself. The cells are compact: many small ones where the points are dense, a few large ones where they are sparse. They hold about the same number of points each once there are more cells than dense places (clusters of points). With fewer cells than dense places a cell takes in whole clusters, large and small, and the counts are about as uneven as under "kmeans". density_power = 0 weights every point alike, which is the objective of "kmeans"; a power above 1 goes past equal counts and gives the cells of dense places fewer points than those of sparse places.

A ladder starts at 2 cells, so its low levels are usually below the number of dense places, and the columns cell_n_min and cell_n_median show where the two kinds part.

The density kind is the default. The default size, 4.5 rows per cell, puts the count above the number of dense places on a layer whose clusters hold more than a few observations each, so the default kind and the default count go together. A coarse ladder the caller sets (with levels, large sizes, or the low levels of the automatic ladder) may not, and at those levels the density kind does not even the counts. partition = "kmeans" gives plain k-means cells, from 25 k-means++ starts unless nstart says otherwise.

init says how each of the nstart starts is drawn before it is refined; the best start is kept. "kmeans++" draws the centres one at a time, each a point taken in proportion to its squared distance from the centres already drawn (times its weight, under "density"), which spreads the start over the points. "random" draws k distinct locations at random, as kmeans() does.

A start of the kind "kmeans" is refined by kmeans() (Hartigan and Wong), for at most 50 iterations from a k-means++ start and 100 from a random one. A start of the kind "density" is refined by Lloyd's iteration, for at most 100 steps: each point goes to its nearest centre, each centre moves to the weighted mean of its points, and a centre left without a point stays where it is. iter_max sets another limit. The start with the lowest sum is kept (under the density kind a later start replaces an earlier one only when its sum is lower by more than one part in ten million, so of starts whose sums agree to rounding the first is kept), and a kept start that was cut off at the limit is reported (see "Conditions"): its centres are those of the last step. A large layer can need more steps than the default limit.

The density kind depends on the points alone. It works on the distinct locations in coordinate order (see below for first coordinates equal but for their last bits), so the order of the rows does not matter. Its tolerances do not depend on the unit of the coordinates: the neighbour distance is not taken below a millionth of the extent of the points (the diagonal of their bounding box), the iteration stops when no centre moves by \(10^{-12}\) of it, and the tie rules below are fractions of the extent or of the quantities they compare. On gridded locations many points are equally near two neighbours or two centres, and the last bits of the coordinates, which move with the unit and the origin, would settle those ties. So squared distances within one part in ten million of each other count as equal, a tie between neighbours goes to the lower first coordinate and then the lower second, a tie between centres goes to the lower-numbered one (between centres a squared distance ties with the least when it is no more than the square of the least distance lengthened by a margin, plus one part in ten million of the least squared distance; the margin is one part in 1e10 of the largest coordinate of the centres, at most a millionth of the diagonal of their bounding box and at least four times the spacing of doubles at that coordinate), first coordinates within that part of the extent count as equal when the rows and the locations are put in order, and so do weights within that part of each other when the first k-means++ centre is drawn. The cells are then the same in another unit or with another origin as long as no coordinate moves by more than about a two-hundred-millionth of the distance between neighbouring locations, but for one case: the margin of the centres grows with their largest coordinate (about 0.46 mm at a UTM northing near 4,550 km, about half a micrometre once the origin lies next to data 5 km across), and the rows are given to the centres in the layer's own coordinates, so a row whose distances to two centres differ by less than the margin with one origin and by more with another goes to the lower-numbered centre with the first and to the nearer with the second. The rounding PROJ leaves when it changes the unit or the false origin, about \(10^{-9}\) m, is below that for locations more than about a quarter of a metre apart. Coordinates rounded more coarsely can give other cells: a lattice at 250 m with its coordinates stored in feet to four decimals does. Points at one location count as that many points at it and share a cell; the neighbour distance is measured to the density_k-th nearest other location, so it is not zero where locations repeat. The neighbour searches use FNN when it is installed. The result is the same without it; the search then takes time that grows with the square of the number of points.

The kind "kmeans" meets the same ties inside kmeans(), which settles them by the last bits of the coordinates and takes no tolerance. So it is handed the coordinates centred on the middle of their bounding box, divided by its diagonal and rounded to \(2^{-30}\) of it (about a billionth); the starts are drawn from those coordinates and ranked by their sums, and the cells it returns are read back in the layer's own coordinates, so the centres, wss and every column are in its unit. The rows are put in order as for the density kind. The cells are then the same in another unit or with another origin unless the change moves a coordinate across the middle of a rounding step, which the rounding PROJ leaves (about \(10^{-9}\) m) does more often the smaller the extent. Distinct locations that would round to one point keep their coordinates unrounded, so they stay distinct. stats::kmeans() also settles such ties by the last bits of its own compiled arithmetic, which differ between platforms, so on a layer where ties decide cells the kind "kmeans" can return other cells on another platform from the same coordinates and seed, and with them every column read off the cells.

The columns keep their meaning under "density", because each is read off the cells and not off the way they were drawn. wss is the within-cell sum of squares of the coordinates with every point counted once, taken about each cell's mean, so wss and elbow compare between kinds; the weighted sum the centres minimise is kept in attr(, "partition")$objective, and wss_spread is its spread over the starts. cp, moran_z and the test against one cell need cells drawn without the response, which both kinds give. reliability is computed for square cells of the level's average area and count and never reads the cells, so it is the same number under either kind. The elbow is found more readily under "density" where the points cluster: once each cluster has its centres, further centres go into the clusters, the sparse ground between them keeps its sum of squares, and the curve flattens.

A profile of the density kind, or of either kind from random starts, carries attr(, "partition"), and select_resolution(), the seeding functions and build_tessellation() hand that record on with the cells (see "Value"). A result with no such record was built by plain k-means: from k-means++ starts when it comes from a profile, and from random starts when a seeding function fitted it.

The ladder and its bounds

This is the ladder of a call that sets levels, n_levels, min_cell_n, sample_n or range_floor, or passes obs_per_cell = NULL, and of a call with no estimate: one without a response, with predictor_vars, or with a logical or wholly missing response. Cells are clusters of the (projected) coordinates of the kind partition names, fitted at each level as the best of nstart k-means++ starts (see determine_optimal_levels for why) unless init says otherwise (see "The partition"). Levels are spaced logarithmically, because cell diameter scales as \(L^{-1/2}\): a unit step wastes fits at large \(L\) and starves resolution at small. The ladder runs from 2 to a ceiling the data impose. The ceiling is floor(n / min_cell_n): cells with fewer than min_cell_n rows on average have too little support. With a response_var, \(n\) is the number of rows of the layer (not of the subsample) that are scored: those with a response and, with predictor_vars, every predictor, since the cell means the criteria read are built from those rows alone. ceiling_from is then "min_cell_n (rows with a response)" when some rows are not scored (the label is the same when it is a predictor they lack), and a warning of class spatialkit_response_ceiling gives both counts and names the bound in force. Without a response_var, or when no row has a response, \(n\) is every point. The ceiling is also held to the number of distinct locations, one cell on each, and to one short of the number of points, which stats::kmeans() needs. The count \(n / L\) is the rows per cell only when the scored rows are spread over the whole extent. Where they sit in one part of it, the cells elsewhere hold none and the occupied cells hold more than \(n / L\), so the ceiling is lower than those cells need: cells_resp and cell_resp_mean give the cells that hold a scored row and the scored rows per such cell at each level (of the subsample, when the cells are fitted to one), and profiling the scored rows alone bounds the ladder by the area they cover.

When fewer than two cells meet min_cell_n (floor(n / min_cell_n) < 2), or the layer has one distinct location, there is no ladder: the profile scores two cells so that level is still visible (or the levels asked for, as given), supported is FALSE, ceiling_from is "fewer than two supported cells" (or "fewer than two distinct locations") and a warning of class spatialkit_not_supported names both numbers.

min_cell_n sets the ceiling of this ladder. It is a mean number of rows per cell and not a minimum: a cell of a level at the ceiling can hold fewer (cell_n_min). It is floored to a whole number, so 4.5 is read as 4. With levels it does not choose the levels scored, and it still sets bounds$ceiling, supported and the spatialkit_not_supported warning.

The range floor is ceiling(area / range^2) when an autocorrelation range is available: cells wider than the range average over more than one patch of the field. It is reported in the bounds and the print, and by default it is not applied: the ladder starts at 2. When the layer supports the floor and it lies between the ladder's ends, the floor is one of the ladder's levels all the same (so the ladder can have one more level than n_levels): select_resolution(criterion = "reliability") reads from the floor up and returns the floor itself, not the next level the spacing happened to put above it. The range is an estimate, and a response with no spatial structure can still be given one, so a ladder started at the floor can leave out the coarse counts such a response supports. range_floor = TRUE starts the ladder at the floor when the layer supports it and it lies below the ceiling. When the floor exceeds the ceiling the data cannot support a tessellation that respects their own correlation structure; that is reported as a finding (a warning of class spatialkit_not_supported, and attr(x, "bounds")$supported is FALSE) and the ladder runs from 2 to the ceiling (or the levels asked for are scored, as given), so the profile still shows what each level costs. A floor equal to the ceiling would leave one level and nothing to compare it with, so that ladder starts at 2 as well. On a layer larger than sample_n the ceiling is also held to half the subsample's scored rows (two per cell, the least a fitted cell can be scored on; half the subsample without a response); ceiling_from is then "sample_n", a floor above that is logged with a request to raise sample_n, and it does not make supported FALSE.

The floor moves with the range estimate, and the ceiling with \(n\). To compare profiles of similar data (the folds of a cross-validation, say), pass the same levels to each. reliability is the one criterion that still reads the floor: select_resolution() holds it to the levels at or above the floor by default, so its pick can differ widely between two such profiles when the floor is supported on one and not on the other; pass range_floor = FALSE there to read the whole ladder.

A ladder that obs_per_cell sets is a ladder of sizes (see "Observations per cell"). It has one level per size \(s\), max(2, round(n / s)) cells, held to the most centres k-means can place: the distinct locations, and one short of the points. Its centres are fitted to every row. No subsample is drawn, and n_levels, min_cell_n, sample_n and range_floor are not read. The finest size takes the part min_cell_n has on the ladder above: bounds$ceiling is the finest level, and supported is FALSE when the finest size gives fewer than two cells or the range floor is above the finest level. The range floor is reported and not applied.

A ladder of sizes under sac = "auto" fits no variogram, so cp and reliability are NA at every level there, and attr(, "cp_noise") says why. sac = NULL, or a sac of the caller's own, gives them. sac = "auto" and obs_per_cell = "auto" are the defaults, so the default profile has neither column.

Observations per cell

obs_per_cell sets the ladder by a size: the mean number of rows a cell is to hold. The level of a size \(s\) is max(2, round(n / s)) cells, with \(n\) the rows the size divides (see the argument). A size says how many observations a cell value is to stand on, and that is the caller's choice: no criterion makes it. Under a size neither the cells, which are fitted to the coordinates, nor their number, which is a count of rows, depend on the values of the response. Under select_resolution(criterion = "loo") the count does.

For pooled values the leave-one-out error tends to keep falling as the cells shrink, so its minimum tends to be the finest size offered, and the end of the ladder would then choose the count (see "How this was checked"). select_resolution(criterion = "size") therefore sets the count of pooled values from a size, 4.5 unless another is given, and criterion = "loo" reads the lowest error for plain means.

Two columns say what a size leaves a cell value to stand on. share_alone is the share of the scored rows that are the only scored row of their cell: the plain mean of such a cell is one observation, and its pooled value has the smallest own weight a cell can have. own_weight is the median weight a pooled value gives the cell's own mean: at 1 the pooled values are the plain means, and at 0 each is the mean of the cell's neighbours.

obs_per_cell = "auto", the default, is resolved against the other ladder arguments, in this order. Whether the caller supplied an argument is what counts, so a value a wrapper passes on counts as supplied.

  1. With levels, "auto" is NULL: the levels are scored as given. A numeric obs_per_cell beside levels is an error, since each sets the ladder.

  2. With n_levels, min_cell_n, sample_n or range_floor supplied, "auto" is NULL: those arguments describe the ladder of "The ladder and its bounds", and the caller gets it, with the estimate's columns when there is an estimate.

  3. Otherwise "auto" is 4.5 when the estimate is "pooled", the seven sizes 18, 12, 9, 6, 4.5, 3 and 2 when it is "mean", and NULL without an estimate.

  4. A numeric obs_per_cell beside n_levels, min_cell_n, sample_n or range_floor = TRUE sets the ladder, with a warning of class spatialkit_ladder_unused that names the arguments that are not read.

On a ladder of sizes the centres are fitted to every row and the count of cells grows with the rows, so a step that compares every point with every centre grows with the square of the rows. partition = "kmeans" has such a step in every pass and in a k-means++ start. partition = "density" has it in a k-means++ start and, without FNN, in every pass; with FNN and init = "random" it has none. The profile stops before any fit, with an error of class spatialkit_work_limit, when the points times the cells of the finest level times nstart (times iter_max for the density kind without FNN) is above getOption("spatialkit.fit_work_max", 1e10). The message names the ways on: fewer starts, which keep the best of fewer; a coarser size; partition = "density" with init = "random", which leaves a cell without a point more often (see spatialkit_empty_cells under "Conditions") and, where FNN could not be loaded, needs it reinstalled first; or a higher limit. The work and the limit are written in full, so that a work just above the limit does not print as the limit. The limit counts the finest level, and a ladder of several sizes fits every one of its levels. At the default size the work grows with the square of the rows, and a call just below the limit runs for a long time and prints nothing while it runs. spatialkit-options describes both limits.

Without FNN the density kind also finds its weights by comparing every pair of distinct locations. A profile on a ladder of sizes stops, with the same class, when the square of their number is above getOption("spatialkit.exact_pairs_max", 2e9), which is about 44,700 locations. The result of every search is the same with and without the package. moran_i and moran_z need FNN and Matrix at a level where more than 5,000 cells hold a scored row. Without them a ladder of sizes has NA in both columns there, with a warning of class spatialkit_moran_skipped, and so does a ladder set any other way (see "Conditions"). At a level of up to 5,000 such cells, when either package is missing, the neighbour weights of the cell means are held as a dense matrix of cells by cells.

The criteria

select_resolution() reads cp by default on a profile without an estimate; on one with an estimate it reads the size (pooled values) or loo (plain means). reliability needs a variogram range and is NA without one; elbow is NA unless the points cluster; and moran_z is a diagnostic of the cell means, which no function reads as a count rule by default. With an estimate the profile has a fifth column, loo, which is the last entry. Each entry below says what the column measures and what it returns.

elbow

How far the WSS curve sags below a power law: on log-log axes, \(\log\) WSS below the straight line from \(k = 1\) (the total sum of squares) to the last level, in natural-log units (larger is better). Points with no cluster structure have a WSS close to \(c/k\), which is straight on those axes, so the column is NA at every level unless the largest sag reaches \(\log 1.25\), and the print says there is no elbow (the rule is given in determine_optimal_levels). The classical chord on linear axes found a "knee" on such a layer anyway, at about \(\sqrt{L_{first} L_{last}}\), where the ladder's ends put it. A level whose WSS is 0 (to within \(10^{-12}\) of the total), one cell on every distinct location, which the ladder reaches when locations repeat, is left out of the line; when the other levels have no elbow, that fall to zero is the elbow, and its sag is measured with the WSS floored at \(10^{-12}\) of the total, which puts it far above any other level's. Geometry only; it knows nothing of the response. It is NA unless the points cluster, and where they do it names the number of clusters, which is usually the first level or two of the ladder.

cp

Mallows' \(C_p\) of the piecewise-constant approximation of the response (or of its OLS residuals on predictor_vars) by cell means: \(RSS(L)/n + 2 \tau^2 L / n\), with \(\tau^2\) the nugget of the fitted variogram (lower is better). It estimates the error of re-measuring the sampled sites: each scored row observed again at its own location, with fresh noise of variance \(\tau^2\), and predicted by the mean of its cell. For an observation at a new location the penalty needs the spread of the field inside a cell as well, which the nugget leaves out. This \(\tau^2\) is the nugget, the noise of one measurement; it is not the tau2 of a pooled value, which is the mean squared distance between a cell's level and its target. When the cells are fitted to a subsample of \(m\) of the \(N\) points with a response, the penalty is split between the two: \(RSS(L)/m + \tau^2 L_m / m + \tau^2 L / N\), where the first two terms estimate the approximation error from the subsample (adding back the optimism of its own cell means, over the \(L_m\) cells its scored points fall in) and the last is the variance of cell means built from all \(N\), which is what the tessellation will carry. With no subsample it is the formula above. On a smooth field with little noise the approximation keeps improving as cells shrink and the penalty is too small to stop it, so the minimum of \(C_p\) is the support ceiling and min_cell_n is what is choosing; select_resolution() says so when that happens. \(C_p\) has an interior minimum when the nugget is a large share of the sill. A nugget of 0, or of at most \(10^{-4}\) of the sill, which estimate_sac_range() marks as nugget_at_bound, is the fit's lower bound and not an estimate, and as \(\tau^2\) it would leave no penalty, so that \(C_p\) would descend to the ceiling whatever the field: \(C_p\) does not take it. When the variogram gives no nugget (none was fitted, its nugget is at that bound, its fit has no minimum inside the ranges searched, its range is below the shortest lag, it found no spatial structure, or sac is a range alone), \(\tau^2\) is Mallows' own choice instead: the residual mean square \(RSS / (m - L_m)\) of the finest level whose cells hold at least two scored rows on average. It counts the structure within those cells as noise too, so on average it is no smaller than the nugget and errs towards fewer cells. When no level's cells hold that many, or the finest that does has a residual mean square of 0 to within the rounding of the values scored (as when each of its cells holds one location whose rows carry one value), cp is NA at every level, as it is for a constant response, which the profile warns about. Whatever its source, \(\tau^2\) is held to the semivariance of nearest-neighbour pairs the variogram carries (attr(sac, "short_lag_semivariance"), see sac_nugget): a semivariance does not fall as the lag shrinks, so it bounds the nugget from above, and a larger \(\tau^2\) is contradicted by the closest pairs and stops \(C_p\) early. A semivariance of 0 holds nothing. When \(\tau^2\) is not the nugget as it stands, a warning of class spatialkit_cp_noise says where it came from, and attr(, "cp_noise") records the source and, when the semivariance held it, the number it replaced. Its minimum is often a bound, the support ceiling when the nugget is a small share of the sill, and select_resolution() then names the bound in edge. The same formula at one cell, with the total sum of squares as its RSS, is kept in attr(, "one_cell"), with the p-value at every level of the F test of that level's cell means against one mean. A level has to beat one cell: select_resolution() returns structured = FALSE when \(C_p\) at one cell is within tol of the optimum, or when the cell means at the optimum differ from one mean by no more than chance allows, because one mean for the whole layer then predicts as well as the cells and the count is not identified (see select_resolution for the rule).

moran_z

A diagnostic of the cell means: the standardised deviate of Moran's I on the cell means, or with predictor_vars on the residuals of the cell means regressed on the cell-mean predictors, over the 8 nearest neighbours of each cell. It tests whether neighbouring cell means are independent. It does not measure what the cells leave unexplained, and it does not say how well they represent the response. On any autocorrelated response it grows as the cells get finer than the range, because neighbouring cells then resemble each other, and it has almost no power below about 20 cells, where the 8-neighbour graph between cells is close to complete and Moran's I sits near \(-1/(L - 1)\) whatever the data. The level with the smallest \(|z|\) is therefore among the coarsest it is computed at on a structured response, whatever the layer and its ceiling, and arbitrary on a response with no structure, where \(z\) is calibrated and flat in \(L\). select_resolution() refuses to read it as a criterion unless asked with diagnostic = TRUE, and neither summary() nor the functions that take a profile as a cell count read it by default. NA at nine cells or fewer.

reliability

The between-cell signal's share of the spread in the cell means, from the fitted variogram alone via Krige's additivity relation (Cressie 1996), for square cells of the level's average area holding the level's average share of the layer's points with a response (larger is better). This is the shrinkage factor of Fay and Herriot (1979). The curve has an interior optimum, a broad one, which can lie below the range floor. select_resolution() reads it at the levels at or above the floor (its range_floor argument), and what it returns is then often the floor, which is a level of every ladder the profile builds: the coarsest count the range allows, with the range choosing rather than the curve. Report the flat region with the count. The domain term is taken over the convex hull the area is measured on, so rotating the layer does not move it. NA without a usable variogram, and when the variogram's range was rejected (see sac).

loo

With an estimate: the leave-one-out mean squared error of that cell value (lower is better). It estimates the squared error of predicting one further observation, at a location drawn the way the data's locations were, by the value of the cell it falls in. That error depends on the cell value, so the column is computed for the estimate the profile is given and for no other. Each scored row of the layer is predicted by the value of its cell computed without it, in the cell of its nearest centre, which is the cell the seeds will build. Under "mean" a row in a cell of two or more is predicted by the mean of the others, and a row alone in its cell by the mean of the cell of its nearest other scored row. Under "pooled" the cell's mean and its own weight are computed again without the row; the spread inside the cells, the spread between a cell and its target and the targets are held; and a cell left empty takes its target. It needs no variogram. It describes locations among the observations and says nothing of a location away from them: it is a criterion for comparing levels where data are near, not an estimate of the error of a map. loo_se is the standard error, over rows, of that level's mean squared error. It is not the standard error of a difference between two levels, whose errors come from the same rows. scored_per_cell counts the rows loo read, every scored row of the layer, over the cells that hold one; cell_resp_mean counts the rows the other response criteria read, which are the subsample's when the cells are fitted to one. For pooled values its minimum tends to be the finest size offered (see "How this was checked"), so a size sets the count, and select_resolution(criterion = "size") reads it.

cp and reliability answer different questions: how well the cells represent the field, and whether the cell values are distinguishable from noise. They can disagree, and the profile shows both.

Conditions

What changes the meaning of a result is raised as an R warning with a class, so tryCatch(), withCallingHandlers() and options(warn = 2) see it without matching message text; the rest is logged (see spatialkit_quiet). These are the classes this function raises; spatialkit-conditions lists every class the package raises.

spatialkit_not_supported

supported is FALSE, because the range floor exceeds the ceiling or because fewer than two cells meet min_cell_n.

spatialkit_response_ceiling

Rows that are not scored (no response, or with predictor_vars a predictor missing) lowered the ceiling. The message names the bound in force, min_cell_n or, on a subsample, sample_n; the condition carries n, n_response, ceiling, ceiling_from, n_sample and n_scored.

spatialkit_constant_response

The scored variable is constant to within rounding (a response the predictors fit exactly leaves such residuals), so cp, moran_i and moran_z are NA at every level. On a profile with an estimate whose rows are constant too, so are loo and loo_se, and for pooled values own_weight; the message names them. summary() of such a profile stops with an error that says the response is constant. Both tests read the raw values and, where those show no spread, the values centred on their median and scaled, so 1e15 plus a spread of 1 is not constant while values that differ only by their rounding (0.1 beside 0.3 / 3) are; residuals are read against the rounding of the regression and of the response, and where the residuals of the raw values show no spread, they are those of a fit to the response less its median. The test for cp reads the scored rows of the subsample and the estimate's every row of the layer (of its selection half under select_on = "split") with a value: where the first finds the response constant and the second does not, the message says that loo is scored, and the print does not call the response a constant.

spatialkit_empty_cells

Under partition = "density": a centre holds no point, so there are fewer occupied cells than the count. A centre that loses its points stays where it is, and the start that is kept is the one with the lowest sum, whether or not all its centres hold points. It happens at high counts, mostly from init = "random". The condition carries level, the count, and empty.

spatialkit_not_converged

The start that was kept was cut off at the iteration limit, so its centres are those of the last step and a longer run can still move points between cells. Not raised for the kind "kmeans" from k-means++ starts under iter_max = NULL. The condition carries level (every level it happened at), iter and iter_max. Raise iter_max.

spatialkit_ladder_unused

A numeric obs_per_cell sets the ladder, and the caller also supplied n_levels, min_cell_n, sample_n or range_floor = TRUE, which are then not read. The condition carries unused (the argument names) and obs_per_cell.

spatialkit_size_not_reached

On a ladder of sizes: a size does not give the count it asks for. Either a size given as a number gives fewer than two cells while a finer one does not, and its level is 2 (reason is "fewer than two cells"); or a size asks for more cells than k-means can place, and its level is the most that can (reason is "more cells than can be placed"). It is raised once for each reason, naming every size held for it. The condition carries obs_per_cell and wanted (one element for each such size, in the order of the ladder), used and reason. When the finest size gives fewer than two cells the warning is spatialkit_not_supported, with obs_per_cell among its fields and min_cell_n NA; and spatialkit_response_ceiling is not raised on such a ladder, since a size already counts the rows with a response.

spatialkit_repeated_locations

With an estimate: scored rows share a location. Each row is left out alone and the others at its location stay, so loo then describes a further observation at a place already observed. Raised once, after the levels are scored, and not when loo is NA at every level. The condition carries n (the rows that share a location), total (the rows loo read) and column.

spatialkit_no_scored_rows

Under select_on = "split": no row of the selection half has a response, and the rows of the layer with one are all in the estimation half. rss, cp, moran_i and moran_z, which read the selection half, are NA at every level. With an estimate, whose check that it has rows to read is made on the layer, loo and the estimate's other columns read no row and are NA at every level too. With predictor_vars a row counts when it has a response and every predictor. Not raised when no row of the layer has a response. Raised once, after the levels are scored. The condition carries reason ("no response in the selection half"), n (0, the rows of the selection half scored), selection (the rows of the selection half), n_response (the rows of the layer with a response) and column. Raised too, with or without the split, when rows of the layer have a response and none of them every predictor: then reason is "no row with a response and every predictor", n_response the rows with a finite response, and selection NA without the split.

spatialkit_pool_unavailable

With an estimate: the values of the response lie beyond what the arithmetic of the estimate holds, values so large, or so close to their median, that the squares of many such values can overflow or lose their precision, so loo, loo_se and own_weight are NA at every level. Where the test for cp finds such a response constant, cp, moran_i and moran_z are NA for the same reason, and this message names them in place of spatialkit_constant_response. The message gives the bounds; the response rescaled by a power of ten is scored. Raised once, after the levels are scored. The condition carries reason ("values out of range") and columns, the response, as summarize_by_cell(estimate = "pooled") raises the class for its pooled columns.

spatialkit_moran_skipped

With a level of more than 5,000 cells, on any ladder, when FNN cannot be loaded or Matrix is not installed: moran_i and moran_z are NA at a level where more than 5,000 cells hold a scored row, and every other column is computed. Raised once, before the first fit, when such a level can occur: the cells that hold a scored row are counted after a level's fit, so where rows without a response leave fewer of them the two columns are computed after all. The condition carries limit, levels (the levels above the limit) and missing.

spatialkit_variogram_unusable

The variogram, the one estimated or sac, gives no usable range (rejected_reason of estimate_sac_range()), so reliability is NA, and the message says whether cp may still take its nugget. The condition carries reason, converged (whether the variogram model converged; NA when it does not say), nugget and nugget_used.

spatialkit_cp_noise

cp does not take the variogram's nugget as it stands. Its noise variance is the residual mean square of the finest level (the variogram gives no nugget, or its nugget is at the fit's lower bound), or the semivariance of nearest-neighbour pairs, which holds the nugget or that residual mean square where they are larger; or there is none and cp is NA at every level: the finest level whose cells hold two scored rows on average has a residual mean square of 0 to within rounding, or, with the nugget at its bound, no level's cells hold that many. The condition carries source, value and level (as attr(, "cp_noise") holds them; with no noise variance source and value are NA, and level is the level whose residual mean square is 0 to within rounding, or NA), cap (the semivariance, NA when the variogram carries none), uncapped_source and uncapped_value (what cp would take without the hold, and with no noise variance what it refused: the nugget at its bound, or that residual mean square).

The other warnings of this function (points dropped, a variogram of another variable) are R warnings without a class; rows left out for a missing response, a rising WSS curve and a subsample too small to reach the floor are logged only.

One refusal is an error with a class, spatialkit_work_limit: resolution_profile() stops before a step whose count of comparisons is above a limit. The condition carries work (the count), limit and what (the step). On a ladder that obs_per_cell sets, the count of cells grows with the rows, so two costs are bounded before the variogram is estimated and before any fit. The fits: the points times the cells of the finest level times nstart may not pass getOption("spatialkit.fit_work_max", 1e10) (what = "partition fit"; the condition also carries kind, init, nstart and fnn). That product counts the step in which every point is compared with every centre, which partition = "kmeans" has in every pass and in a k-means++ start, and partition = "density" has in a k-means++ start. Without FNN the density kind compares every point with every centre in every pass, and the product is multiplied by iter_max; with FNN and init = "random" it has no such step and nothing is counted. The density kind's weights: without FNN they come from a search that compares every pair of distinct locations, and the square of their number may not pass getOption("spatialkit.exact_pairs_max", 2e9) (what = "density weights"); density_power = 0 has no weights and no such search. With an estimate and without FNN, on any ladder, the same limit bounds the three exact searches the estimate's columns make: each scored row's nearest centre, each cell's nearest cells, and, under "mean", the nearest other location of a row alone in its cell. The result of every search is the same with and without FNN.

The warnings of the pooled values and of the count record, which summarize_by_cell() raises, are listed on its page.

How this was checked

The sizes for pooled values were compared in a simulation of 200 layers, each 1,500 clustered observations of a field with covariance exp(-d / 100) plus noise on a square of side 1,000 (dev/sim-pooled-values.R in the package's GitHub repository; summarize_by_cell describes it), profiled at the sizes 18, 12, 9, 6, 4.5, 3 and 2 with partition = "density". The lowest loo of the pooled value was at the size 2 on 176 layers, at 3 on 22 and at 4.5 on 2. That of the plain mean was at 2 on none: it was at 6 on 86 layers, at 4.5 on 51, at 9 on 49, at 12 on 12, and at 18 and at 3 on one each. These figures are of those seven sizes and say nothing of another ladder.

References

Cressie, N. (1996). Change of support and the modifiable areal unit problem. Geographical Systems, 3(2–3), 159–180.

Fay, R. E. and Herriot, R. A. (1979). Estimates of income for small places: an application of James-Stein procedures to census data. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 74(366), 269–277. doi:10.1080/01621459.1979.10482505

Mallows, C. L. (1973). Some comments on \(C_p\). Technometrics, 15(4), 661–675. doi:10.1080/00401706.1973.10489103

See also

select_resolution() to read a level and its flat region off the profile; summary.resolution_profile() for every criterion's pick side by side; determine_optimal_levels() for a count from the coordinates alone; build_tessellation() and get_voronoi_seeds(), which accept the profile or a select_resolution() result directly as approx_n_cells and n.

Other resolution: determine_optimal_levels(), plot.resolution_profile(), select_resolution(), summary.resolution_profile()

Examples

library(sf)
# An exponential field with range parameter 200 (true effective range
# 600 m) on a 1 km square, with a nugget of 0.6 on a unit sill.
set.seed(4)
n <- 400
xy <- data.frame(x = 5e5 + runif(n, 0, 1000), y = 5e6 + runif(n, 0, 1000))
D  <- as.matrix(dist(xy))
xy$z <- as.numeric(t(chol(exp(-D / 200) + diag(0.6, n))) %*% rnorm(n))
pts <- st_as_sf(xy, coords = c("x", "y"), crs = 32632)

# The default profile: one level at 4.5 rows per cell, scored for
# pooled values, in density-weighted cells, with no variogram.
prof1 <- resolution_profile(pts, response_var = "z")
prof1
#> Resolution profile: 1 level on 400 points
#>   ladder      : 89 cells (obs_per_cell = 4.5 on the 400 rows with a response; centres fitted to every row; floor 2 (no range))
#>   variogram   : none fitted: a size ladder fits one only when `sac` is given (cp and reliability are NA)
#>   scored on   : response; 3 density-weighted k-means++ starts (power 1, 8 neighbours) per level
#>   one cell    : rss 490 (one mean for the layer; a level has to beat it)
#>   estimate    : pooled toward the 8 nearest cells; loo on 400 rows of the layer; one cell: loo 1.23
#> 
#>  levels    wss wss_spread elbow cell_n_min cell_n_median cell_diam_median rss
#>      89 502000     0.0698    NA          1             4               64 255
#>  cp moran_i moran_z reliability cells_resp cell_resp_mean scored_per_cell   loo
#>  NA   0.389    8.28          NA         89           4.49            4.49 0.903
#>  loo_se share_alone own_weight
#>  0.0645        0.01      0.397
select_resolution(prof1)   # the count the size gives
#> Resolution by size: 89 cells
#>   size        : 4.5 rows per cell, the default (obs_per_cell); 400 rows / 89 cells = 4.49
#>   cells       : density-weighted k-means++ starts (power 1, 8 neighbours)
#>   estimate    : pooled toward the 8 nearest cells
#>   at this size: 1.0% of the rows are alone in their cell; median own weight 0.40
#>   loo         : 0.903 (one cell for the layer: 1.23)
#>   note        : the count is set by obs_per_cell = 4.5, the default; no
#>                 criterion chose it.

# A ladder of counts for plain means: n_levels asks for the ladder and
# estimate = NULL scores no cell value, so cp is the rule that goes
# with it.
prof <- resolution_profile(pts, response_var = "z", n_levels = 12,
                           estimate = NULL)
prof
#> Resolution profile: 12 levels on 400 points
#>   ladder      : 2 to 44 cells (floor 4 from range 516.8, not applied, ceiling 44 from min_cell_n = 9)
